note: Every claim below is checked against a generated artifact by scripts/validate-claims.py, which runs as the last step of `make verify`. A claim whose check fails is a build failure, not a downgrade to 'unverified'. Claims not marked 'verified' may not appear in the README, on Devfolio, in the video, or in social copy -- the validator enforces that too.

claims.text: All 18 assertions in the unmodified upstream test suite pass against the Zig library.
claims.limitation: upstream/pdjson/tests/tests.c is compiled in place from the pinned tree and linked against zig-out/lib/libpdjson.a. No copy is made and no line is edited; scripts/verify-upstream-hashes.sh enforces byte-identity independently.

claims.text: Zero assertions in the upstream suite are skipped, adapted, or marked unsupported.
claims.limitation: The suite contains 18 assertions. Passing them is necessary, not sufficient -- which is why the differential corpus exists.

claims.text: The upstream source tree is byte-identical to commit 78fe04b across all 9 files.
claims.limitation: Verifies the committed copy against a SHA-256 manifest. scripts/fetch-upstream.sh re-clones from GitHub at the pinned commit to confirm the copy matches the real upstream.

claims.text: Across 6,104 differential comparisons on the fixed corpus, spanning all four documented input sources and every exported function, the Zig implementation and the pinned C original produce byte-identical behaviour transcripts, with 0 divergences.
claims.limitation: 215 inputs x 27 drive modes, covering json_open_buffer, json_open_string, json_open_stream (FILE*) and json_open_user. Counts only inputs where the original has defined behaviour; the 43 cases where an ASan+UBSan build of the original reports an error are counted separately as upstream_ub.

claims.text: The differential comparison covers 28 drive modes: four input sources crossed with peek, skip, reset, the separator API and strict mode, plus five json_skip_until targets, four allocation-failure schedules, and a mode that calls json_next past the terminal event.
claims.limitation: Sources: json_open_buffer, json_open_stream (FILE*), json_open_user. Modes: next, nostream, peek, skip, sep, oom:0/1/2/5. Documented in docs/transcript-schema.md.

claims.text: Differential testing and the oracle determinism gate found three defects in the pinned original, all reported upstream with minimal public-API reproducers: a null dereference and an out-of-bounds read at pdjson.c:912, a 0xFF/EOF confusion in the buffer source, and an uninitialised read in json_get_number.
claims.command: make differential && cc -fsanitize=address,undefined -I upstream/pdjson -o /tmp/r tests/upstream-bugs/repro_oom_stack.c upstream/pdjson/pdjson.c && /tmp/r
claims.limitation: Confirmed against the pinned upstream by ASan and UBSan, with a minimal public-API reproducer in tests/upstream-bugs/repro_oom_stack.c. Analysis in docs/upstream-bug-oom-stack.md. Reported upstream; the issue URL is recorded in artifacts/upstream-issues.json.

claims.text: The memory-buffer source in the pinned original treats byte 0xFF as end-of-input on signed-char targets, disagreeing with its own FILE* source on identical input.
claims.limitation: 0xFF is never valid UTF-8, so this changes which error is reported, the byte position, and whether json_source_get() can advance -- it does not make the parser accept invalid input. Analysis in docs/upstream-bug-0xff.md.

claims.text: The Zig static library is built only from Zig-produced objects, exports all 22 public symbols from the pinned header, and contains no upstream parser code.
claims.limitation: Checks archive membership, absence of pdjson.c's 23 internal symbols, absence of undefined json_* imports, presence of all 22 exports, and that no Zig build input references pdjson.c. The archive holds the library object plus, on Linux, Zig's compiler-rt -- bundled so a plain cc/ld can link it without zig cc supplying those helpers.

claims.text: The Zig declarations and the pinned C header agree on every struct offset, size, alignment and enumerator, with sizeof(struct json_stream) == 272 on this target.
claims.limitation: Verified on the host target (arm64 macOS) and in CI on x86-64 Linux. Both tables are derived from the same header on each side, so the check tracks the platform's C ABI rather than hard-coding one; it attests only to targets it has been run on.

claims.text: A C program that includes the pinned public header and declares struct json_stream by value links against only the Zig archive and passes its checks.
claims.limitation: tests/original/abi_consumer.c exercises events, depth, context, raw number lexemes, number values, error text, line numbers, streaming with reset, skip, and json_isspace.

claims.text: The shipped library uses no @constCast, no inline assembly, no @setRuntimeSafety, no unreachable, and no force-unwraps; its 10 pointer casts are confined to the C allocator and char* boundaries and are individually enumerated.
claims.limitation: Zig has no 'unsafe' keyword, so the report defines the term explicitly and lists every occurrence with file and line. Scope is src/ -- the shipped library. Budgets are exact, so an increase requires editing the scanner.

claims.text: The shipped artifact is built in ReleaseSafe, so bounds checks and overflow checks are active at runtime, including in the reported benchmark figures.
claims.limitation: A bare `zig build` produces ReleaseSafe by design (DECISIONS.md D-10). ReleaseFast numbers are reported alongside, not instead.

claims.text: All 12 deliberately injected defects in the Zig implementation are detected by the fixed-corpus differential, with zero survivors.
claims.limitation: Cases where an ASan+UBSan build of the original reports an error are excluded from the comparison, because every mutant trivially differs there. Earlier runs that did not exclude them produced a false 12/12; see DECISIONS.md D-17.

claims.text: Both transcript producers are deterministic: five runs over every fixture in five modes produce byte-identical output.
claims.limitation: Transcripts deliberately exclude pointer values, heap addresses, timing, and errmsg bytes past the NUL terminator, none of which are reproducible. See docs/transcript-schema.md.

claims.text: The Zig implementation's json_get_number matches C strtod bit for bit across a 661-point exponent sweep, powers of two, digit strings up to 500 digits, 20,000 randomised decimal lexemes and 20,000 randomised hex floats.
claims.limitation: Asserted by tests/port/number_torture.zig, which fails the build on any mismatch; the artifact reference here is a proxy because Zig's test runner does not emit JSON. Two documented exceptions: nan(...) payloads that overflow 64 bits are implementation-defined per C99 7.20.1.3p4 and are not matched (D-09). The hex-float path is implemented in this project rather than delegated, because std.fmt.parseFloat truncates past 53 bits of mantissa -- found by fuzzing at ~30M cases (D-18).

claims.text: The Zig implementation is slower than the C original on 9 of the 12 benchmark workload/mode pairs measured, and faster on 3.
claims.limitation: This is an honest mixed result, not a win. Ratios are C median / Zig median on arm64 macOS, 5 repetitions, binaries interleaved within each repetition, all raw per-iteration samples in bench/results/raw.json. The one large Zig win (malformed-early) is dominated by setup rather than parsing and should not be read as throughput. Methodology and the profiling that explains the remaining gap are in bench/methodology.md.

claims.text: A published 30-minute differential fuzz session of 11,812,800 cases, spanning all three input sources, found zero divergences, zero crashes and zero timeouts.
claims.limitation: Exact duration, seed, rounds, case count, rate and mode list are recorded in the session log referenced by artifacts/verification-report.json. Modes cover json_open_buffer, json_open_stream and json_open_user. Allocation-failure modes are excluded from the fuzz defaults because the original crashes constantly there and swamps the signal; they are covered exhaustively by the fixed corpus and by tests/port/allocator_failure.zig. The harness refuses to start unless both binaries produce a valid transcript for a trivial document (DECISIONS.md D-20).

claims.text: Behavioural equivalence is demonstrated for all three documented input sources: json_open_buffer, json_open_stream (FILE*) and json_open_user.
claims.limitation: This was the project's largest gap and is now closed. Both transcript producers select the source by a mode prefix and drive the identical script through each. It matters because upstream issue #37 is precisely a case where two sources disagree on identical bytes, so a single-source comparison would have missed that entire class. Remaining scope: verified on arm64 macOS and x86-64 Linux.

claims.text: On the independent nst/JSONTestSuite conformance corpus, the Zig port and the pinned C original agree on all 318 parsing cases across 11 drive modes and all three input sources, and the original is fully conforming (95/95 must-accept, 188/188 must-reject).
claims.limitation: JSONTestSuite is MIT-licensed and fetched on demand rather than vendored, so this step is skipped when it is absent and `make verify` still succeeds offline; the generated report is committed as evidence. The corpus is used to separate 'the port is wrong' from 'the original is wrong' from 'the standard leaves it open' -- it is not a pass/fail gate on the port. Its i_ cases are implementation-defined and counted as conforming either way.

claims.text: No divergence has ever been observed on any input where the pinned original is well defined: 6,104 fixed-corpus comparisons plus 3,498 JSONTestSuite comparisons plus an 11.8-million-case fuzz session, all at zero.
claims.limitation: Scoped to the buffer input source (see C-18) and to the host and CI targets. 'Well defined' is decided mechanically by an ASan+UBSan build of the original, not by judgement (DECISIONS.md D-16).

claims.text: Verification found two real defects in this port -- a hex-float rounding error and an uninitialised read inherited from the original -- both fixed, regression-tested and documented.
claims.limitation: The first was found by the published fuzz session at ~30M cases; the second by the oracle determinism gate on Linux, which is also upstream #38. Reported here because verification that has never found anything in its own subject is not evidence that anything was checked. See DECISIONS.md D-18 and D-19.

claims.text: Both transcript producers are deterministic on Linux and macOS: five runs over every fixture in five modes produce byte-identical output.
claims.limitation: This gate failed on Linux on first run and that failure was a real upstream defect (#38), not a harness problem. Values that are indeterminate in the original -- errmsg bytes past the NUL, and json_get_number over an unterminated token -- are excluded from the transcript by a rule computed from the public API and applied identically on both sides.

claims.text: The Zig type declarations and the pinned C header describe the same ABI on 6 targets spanning 32- and 64-bit, little-endian ARM, x86, RISC-V and Windows.
claims.limitation: Compile-time comparison, not execution: Zig's layout per target is read via @compileLog and asserted against the pinned header with _Static_assert compiled for that target. Both sides use the Zig toolchain's clang, so it is not a claim about other compilers on those targets -- scripts/abi-check.sh covers the host compiler by executing both probes. sizeof(struct json_stream) is 272 on the 64-bit targets and 204 on the 32-bit ones. The check asserts field sizes as well as offsets, because a shorter trailing array can otherwise be absorbed by padding; that gap existed in the first version and was found by negative-testing the check.

claims.text: Valgrind memcheck independently confirms both memory defects in the pinned original and finds no further ones; the upstream test suite itself is clean under memcheck.
claims.limitation: Linux only, so it runs in CI rather than in `make verify`. Valgrind detects a class ASan cannot -- uninitialised value propagation, with an origin trace -- which is how it independently confirms #38 (strtod branching on bytes malloc never initialised, origin traced to init_string at pdjson.c:186). The script asserts that both known defects still reproduce, so a silent run cannot be mistaken for a clean one. 'No further defects' is scoped to the fixture corpus and the two reproducers, not a general claim about the library.

claims.text: An implementation-independent invariant checker validates 13,936 transcripts and 6,162,897 records from both implementations against 13 rules, with zero violations on either side.
claims.limitation: Complements rather than replaces the C-vs-Zig comparison: equality catches the two disagreeing, invariants catch both being wrong the same way. Written in Python so it shares no code with either implementation. Each of the 14 violation classes is proved able to fail by a deliberately malformed fixture, checked by --self-test before every sweep. Rules were developed against the C original's output first -- two candidate rules fired on unmodified upstream output and were corrected as wrong rules, not reported as findings. Allocation-failure modes are not run against the C binary because it crashes there (#36).

claims.text: Hex-float conversion in this port is correctly rounded under IEEE-754, verified against an exact-integer reference that shares no code with it, over 200,017 literals concentrated at the rounding boundaries.
claims.limitation: This is correctness under IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-ties-to-even, not merely compatibility with this platform's libc -- the reference computes the result with arbitrary-precision integers and decides rounding by integer comparison, with no floating point in the decision path. Scope: the C99 7.20.1.3 hex-float grammar and binary64 only. The reference itself is checked by 17 hand-derived cases before use. It is a tested reference, not a proof.

claims.text: std.fmt.parseFloat truncates rather than rounds hex floats whose significand needs more than 53 bits; demonstrated on Zig 0.16.0 and on master 0.17.0-dev, with a standalone reproducer. Not filed upstream: ziglang/zig restricts issue creation to collaborators.
claims.limitation: The behaviour is reproduced and judged against an exact-integer reference and against libc, both of which disagree with parseFloat. It is NOT filed: `gh issue create -R ziglang/zig` returns 'Interactions on this repository have been restricted to collaborators only'. There is therefore no issue URL, and no Zig maintainer has confirmed it. Related closed issues (#10737, #20287, #2083, #11477) touch the same area but these cases still fail on master. Because it is unconfirmed by the project, this claim is not permitted in the README, on Devfolio, in the video, or in social copy.

claims.text: All 22 exported functions have their behaviour compared between the two implementations; none is untested.
claims.limitation: Classification is derived by reading the harness and test sources, not asserted. Running it the first time found json_skip_until untested -- exported, symbol-checked and ABI-checked, but never behaviourally compared, and not called by upstream's own tests either. Closed with five new drive modes and five Zig tests. Coverage is not exhaustiveness: every export is exercised, but a driven function can still have untested edge cases.

claims.text: The struct layout the C compiler reads out of the pinned header is asserted against src/abi.zig at compile time, so a layout drift fails `zig build` itself: 27 field offsets and sizes, 11 enumerators, 7 struct size and alignment values.
claims.limitation: The contract compares against a recorded layout, so on its own it cannot notice the recorded layout going stale; scripts/abi-generate.sh --check re-derives it from the header and runs inside scripts/abi-check.sh. It asserts only when the build target is in the ABI class it was generated for (LP64 here); off-class targets are covered by scripts/abi-cross-check.sh instead, and `zig build diagnose` reports which case applies. No layout table can detect two adjacent same-width fields swapped with each other; that case is covered by the behavioural differential.

claims.text: The compile-time ABI contract is demonstrated to be capable of failing: 10 injected layout drifts -- 6 in the recorded C layout, 4 in the port's own declarations -- are each caught by the build, with an unmodified control that builds clean.
claims.limitation: Ten specific drifts, not an exhaustive space of them. The control build and the off-class deferral check are both recorded in the same artifact, because 10/10 would also be the score of a permanently broken build or of a guard that never disengages.

claims.text: The Zig archive exports exactly the 22 functions the pinned header declares -- none missing, none extra -- compared as a set rather than as a count.
claims.limitation: Symbol names and presence only; it says nothing about signatures, which the C consumer link in the same report covers by compiling against the pinned header. Both sides are required to be non-empty, because two empty sets would compare equal.

claims.text: Every escape hatch in the shipped library is classified individually -- 59 occurrences across 8 categories, each matched to a rule keyed by enclosing function rather than by line number, with 0 unclassified.
claims.limitation: The justifications are arguments, not machine-checked proofs. What is mechanically checked is that every occurrence has one, that no forbidden operation is present, and that the inventory matches the current source. The analysis is textual, so a hatch reached through a construct it does not model would be missed. @intCast bounds in particular are argued from the fuzz session and the random-input regression test, not proven.

claims.text: The escape-hatch classifier passes 10 self-tests covering the ways it could silently report the wrong thing, including a hatch mentioned only in a comment, a // inside a string literal, and a test block's scratch being counted as shipped code.
claims.limitation: The artifact check here confirms no forbidden operation is present; the 10 self-test cases run as a gate inside scripts/safety-scan.sh and print their own result rather than writing an artifact. Two of the ten exist because the classifier got those cases wrong first: a test's scratch array was inheriting a justification written about the parser's own state.

claims.text: The Zig port costs a consumer more space than the original: linking one identical C program against the Zig archive rather than the pinned original's object grows the stripped executable 2.42x and the machine-code section 3.29x.
claims.limitation: Measured on arm64 macOS with Apple clang; section names and page rounding differ on ELF, which the script handles but which has not been cross-checked on every target. The comparison links the same consumer source with the same compiler and flags and verifies both binaries produce the same output before reporting, but a larger consumer would dilute the ratio. Archive-vs-object bytes are recorded and deliberately not claimed, because a .a and a .o are not the same kind of object.

claims.text: The parser's transition relation is written out as a 10-state specification derived from RFC 8259 and pdjson.h, and the corpus exercises all 54 specified transitions, with 0 transitions observed that the specification does not contain.
claims.limitation: Single-step transitions under json_next only. peek does not advance the parser and skip consumes a whole value, so neither forms a single-step successor; those are covered by scripts/api-coverage.py instead. The state is derived from json_get_context's type and count, so it distinguishes an object key from an object value but not, say, one malformed input from another -- ERROR is a single event regardless of cause. 100% transition coverage is not path coverage: reaching every edge says nothing about every sequence of edges.

claims.text: Both implementations cover exactly the same set of state transitions on the same inputs: 0 transitions are reached by one and not the other.
claims.limitation: This follows from the transcripts being byte-identical and is therefore a redundant check rather than independent evidence. It is recorded because it is cheap and because a difference here would mean the byte-identity claim had broken somewhere the diff was not looking.

claims.text: All four documented input sources are exercised with real comparison counts, not asserted: json_open_buffer 3,270, json_open_stream 1,090 (a real FILE*), json_open_user 1,090 (caller callbacks), json_open_string 654 -- each at 0 divergences.
claims.limitation: The matrix attributes each drive mode to its json_open_* function and multiplies by the input count; it is derived from the run rather than measured per call, so a mode that silently fell back to a different source would be misattributed. The source functions themselves are separately covered by scripts/api-coverage.py. Upstream's own tests do not drive json_open_stream or json_open_user at all, so these comparisons are the only behavioural evidence for those two.

claims.text: The differential's comparison is demonstrated to be sensitive to every field a transcript record carries -- event, token bytes, token length, number bits, line, position, depth, context, context count, error text, operation and sequence -- by perturbing each field and requiring the comparison to notice.
claims.limitation: The field sensitivity is checked against synthetic transcripts, not against the parser: it proves the comparison notices a changed field, not that the parser can produce every such change. The three deliberately weakened comparators are also checked to be genuinely blind to what they ignore, because a weakening that changed nothing would mean the strength was never there. The artifact check here records which detector produced the report; the field-by-field result prints rather than writing its own artifact.
